endings.text: End of the walk. The Everleigh Club lasted eleven years. On 24 October 1911 the mayor, Carter Harrison Jr., ordered it closed, and Minna took it the way she took everything: "If the Mayor says we must close, that settles it...I'll close up shop and walk out with a smile on my face." The building was razed in July 1933. Prairie Avenue never once admitted that it knew the way to Dearborn Street. It only ever knew the way back.

evidence.text: Chicago's Levee District ran from Eighteenth Street to the north to Twenty-second Street to the south, Wabash to the east and Clark to the west, 'several blocks away from Prairie Avenue'.

evidence.locator: The post's second and last paragraphs.
evidence.text: The Everleigh Club and Vic Shaw's 'resort' were the preeminent brothels in Chicago, 'with Shaw's business existing on Prairie Avenue for a time.' Shaw lived until 1952 in a crumbling mansion at 2906 Prairie Avenue with a dog, cat and parrot.

evidence.reasoning: The blog gives the Levee's bounds as Eighteenth to Twenty-second, Wabash to Clark, 'several blocks away from Prairie Avenue'; the avenues between, Indiana and Michigan, are the city's grid west of Prairie.
evidence.text: The Levee's eastern edge, Wabash Avenue, lay three blocks west of Prairie Avenue, with Indiana and Michigan Avenues between.

The Sisters of the Levee: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Sisters of the Levee: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

evidence.locator: Other Ladies: the Everleigh paragraph; Wikipedia: History.
evidence.text: The sisters were born Simms (in Greene County, Virginia, Ada in 1864 and Minna in 1866; the Kentucky childhood was 'another story concocted by the sisters'). With an inheritance of some $35,000 they ran a house in Omaha, then bought Effie Hankins's brothel at 2131-2133 South Dearborn, and took the name Everleigh from their grandmother, who signed her letters 'Everly yours'. The club opened on February 1, 1900, and turned away many of its first callers.

evidence.locator: Other Ladies: the club paragraph; Wikipedia: History.
evidence.text: The club occupied two mansions, 50 rooms with themes such as the Japanese Throne Room, the Mirror Room and the Silver Parlor; it had 'a $15,000 gold-leafed piano for the Music Room' and '$650 gold cuspidors'. A bottle of champagne cost $12 'in an era when an entire meal could be had for fifty cents', and the entrance fee alone was $50.

evidence.locator: Wikipedia: The sisters' separate responsibilities, Interior layout; Other Ladies.
evidence.text: Ada, the quieter sister, kept the books and hired the women; Minna met the guests. The club employed '15 to 25 cooks and maids', and its women were called 'butterflies'.

On March 3, 1902, Prince Henry of Prussia visited the club; when a slipper came off during a dance and spilled champagne and one of his party drank from it, the custom of drinking champagne from a woman's shoe began.

evidence.reasoning: The church's own structure record dates it 1870-1873 to after 1911 and the 1911 Sanborn sheet draws it at Indiana and Twenty-first; the Levee ran east to Wabash, one block beyond Indiana and Michigan.
evidence.text: First Presbyterian Church stood at Indiana Avenue and Twenty-first Street in 1904, two blocks west of Prairie Avenue and at the Levee's eastern edge.

evidence.locator: Other Ladies: the clients paragraph; Wikipedia: Scandals.
evidence.text: The blog names actor John Barrymore, authors Ring Lardner and Theodore Dreiser, and Marshall Field, Jr. among the club's famed clients, and says rumours persisted for years that the young Field had been shot there; Wikipedia: 'A rival madam maliciously accused the Everleigh sisters of murdering Field.'

Mayor Carter Harrison Jr. ordered the club closed on October 24, 1911. Minna: 'If the Mayor says we must close, that settles it...I'll close up shop and walk out with a smile on my face.' The building was razed in July 1933.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE SISTERS OF THE LEVEE. Dusk on a Monday in November 1904, at Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

Four stops, walking west from Millionaire's Row toward the Levee, the city's red-light district, and ending at a church on its edge. Prairie Avenue is three blocks from the most famous address in Chicago, and it is not the Glessner House. Two sisters who called themselves Everleigh opened a club on Dearborn Street in 1900, and the richest men in the world have found their way to it.

Start at the corner. Watch which way the cabs turn.

armour_corwith_house_1945_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Henry Corwith here. Before them, the Armour household lived here (1890-1891).

armour_house_2115_prairie.text: A stone house with a steep mansard roof, built for the lumberman David Kelley. The family of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour lived here for nearly 50 years. Armour's widow was one of the last people living on the street.

buckingham_house_2036_prairie.text: Clarence Buckingham's house in the 1904 Blue Book. In 1927 his sister Kate will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory, its centre jet throwing water 150 feet up.

coleman_ames_house_1811_prairie.text: A Romanesque house of rough brown sandstone, built in 1886 for Joseph G. Coleman. Cobb and Frost were the architects. It still stands.

dent_house_1823_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas Dent here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

dexter_house_1721_prairie.text: Wirt Dexter's house of 1863, given a new front by Arthur Little in 1889. By 1904 the Blue Book lists Henry H. Walker here.

dexter_house_1721_prairie_frame_house.text: Wirt Dexter's frame house of 1863, the first house on this lot. Arthur Little's brick front on Prairie Avenue was built onto its street end; the old house's own front, porch and bay windows, faces the side yard.

edson_keith_house_1906_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Edson Keith here.

elbridge_keith_house_1900_prairie.text: A limestone house with a steep slate roof, built for Elbridge Keith, a hat merchant who became a banker. The top floor inside that roof was added in the 1880s. It is the last Second Empire house left on Prairie Avenue.

fort_dearborn_massacre_monument_1893.text: A bronze group by Carl Rohl-Smith, paid for by George M. Pullman and set up beside his house in 1893. It shows the Potawatomi leader Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm during the battle of August 1812.

george_glessner_house_1706_prairie.text: Home of George M. Glessner, son of the granite house at 1800; the Glessners built it beside his sister's house at 1700.

glessner_house.text: A granite fortress on the street, with a sunny courtyard inside. People passing by remarked on its narrow windows along 18th Street, not knowing the big ones face the courtyard. By 1904 John and Frances Glessner had lived here since 1887.

glessner_lee_house_1700_prairie.text: Built by the Glessners for their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Decades on she will build the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes still used to train investigators.

goodman_house_1612_prairie.text: Joseph Goodman's stone Italianate of 1869, two years before the Great Fire: round-headed windows under long keystones, and an arched portico at the top of a high stoop.

henderson_house_1816_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Charles M. Henderson here. Before them, W. H. Merrill jr. lived here (1899-1903).

hibbard_house_1701_prairie.text: William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, by William Le Baron Jenney, who fifteen years later built the Home Insurance Building, called the first skyscraper.

high_house_2021_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. James L. High here.

house_1600_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists John G. Shortall here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

house_1608_prairie.text: The Frank household. Henrietta Greenebaum Frank and her sister Hannah Greenebaum Solomon became the first Jewish members of the Chicago Woman's Club in 1876.

house_1616_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William R. Stirling here.

house_1619_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Howard E. Perry here, a clerk by the 1900 census. Before them, Walter H. Wilson lived here (1891).

house_1621_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists John H. Hamline here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

house_1625_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Hugh J. McBirney here.

house_1628_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists M. Einstein here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

house_1634_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists T. H. Bellas here, a commission merchant by the 1900 census. Before them, the Lorimer household lived here (1890-1891).

house_1636_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. H. Morris Johnston here.

house_1828_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Daniel B. Shipman here.

house_2003_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. H. W. Hoyt here. Before them, the Bissell household lived here (1890-1897).

house_2123_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas H. Hulbert here. Before them, the Avery household lived here (1890-1901).

jones_house_1834_prairie.text: A brick Italianate house by John M. Van Osdel, built in 1866 for Fernando Jones, one of Chicago's earliest settlers. In 1886 it gained a mansard roof, to keep up with its neighbors.

keith_house_1808_prairie.text: Osborn R. Keith's granite-fronted house of 1886 by Cobb and Frost, noticed that year at forty thousand dollars, going up as Richardson's granite house rose next door.

kellogg_house_1709_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Jesse Spalding here, a lumberman by the 1900 census. Before them, Mrs. Palmer V. Kellogg lived here (1890-1893).

kellogg_house_1923_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. C. P. Kellogg here. Before them, Pierrepont Isham lived here (1895-1899).

kimball_house_1801_prairie.text: A house in the French château style, built in 1890 for William W. Kimball. He made pianos and organs. Solon S. Beman was the architect.

law_house_1620_prairie.text: Robert Law's house, engraved in 1874 for a series on the homes of Chicago: two storeys over a raised basement under a slated mansard.

marsh_house_1824_prairie.text: Samuel B. Pomeroy's Italianate villa of 1857, one of the oldest houses on the street, hiding behind the stone front George B. Marsh gave it after 1880.

marshall_field_house_1905_prairie.text: Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal. Field is the wealthiest businessman in Chicago, and the street's most famous neighbour.

marshall_field_jr_house_1919_prairie.text: Built in 1867 and made bigger several times. Marshall Field Jr. bought it in 1890. In 1902 D. H. Burnham and Company added a huge new part.

mayer_house_2009_prairie.text: Max A. Meyer's house of 1888, a French Gothic rowhouse by Burnham and Root.

moulton_lowden_house_1912_prairie.text: A big house in the French château style, built in 1882 for B. P. Moulton. In 1898 Frank O. Lowden moved in. He later became governor of Illinois.

otis_house_2033_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists F. R. Otis here.

pullman_house_1729_prairie.text: George M. Pullman's mansion, built between 1870 and 1876. Inside were a theatre for about 200 people, a pipe organ and a bowling alley.

ream_house_1901_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Norman B. Ream here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

rees_house_2110_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Edson Keith jr. here. Before them, Mrs. James H. Rees lived here (1890-1892).

reid_house_2013_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William H. Reid here.

robbins_house_2126_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Edward F. Robbins here. Before them, the Hamill household lived here (1890-1899).

roloson_house_2109_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Robert W. Roloson here. Before them, Mrs. Judith L. Marshall lived here (1890-1899).

rothschild_house_2112_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. M. M. Rothschild here.

sears_meeker_house_1815_prairie.text: Built for Joseph Sears; by 1904 the Blue Book lists Arthur Meeker here.

sherman_house_2100_prairie.text: Built in 1874 for John B. Sherman, who ran the Union Stock Yards. Burnham and Root were the architects. Sherman's daughter Margaret married Daniel Burnham while it was going up.

shortall_gregory_house_1638_prairie_fron.text: Built in 1868. In 1904 the Blue Book lists Robert B. Gregory here.

spalding_house_1637_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William Gold Hibbard jr. here. Before them, the Spalding household lived here (1890-1899).

stone_house_2035_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. H. O. Stone here.

tolman_house_2031_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Samuel A. Tolman here.

tucker_smith_house_2140_prairie.text: Built in 1876. In 1904 the Blue Book lists Byron L. Smith here.

walker_house_1720_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. James M. Walker here. Before them, Miss Jennie Royce lived here (1890-1891).

wheeler_house_1812_prairie.text: A brick row house in the Dutch style, built in 1884 for George H. Wheeler. He owned grain elevators. Burnham and Root designed it.

premise: Three blocks west of the mansions, two sisters from Virginia run the most famous house in Chicago, with gold cuspidors and a $15,000 piano. Prairie Avenue pretends not to know the way.

stage.caption: Two gentlemen in evening coats come round the corner and walk briskly west along Eighteenth Street.

cast.name: A gentleman out for the evening (unnamed)

stops.text: Eighteenth and Prairie, as the lamps come on. Eighteenth Street is a border. To the north and east: the mansions. To the south and west, "several blocks away from Prairie Avenue", begins the Levee, the district that runs from Eighteenth Street to Twenty-second, Wabash to Clark, home of the city's most famous brothels. The ladies of Prairie Avenue never mention it. And yet one of the two most famous houses in Chicago, Vic Shaw's, stood for a time on Prairie Avenue itself. The two gentlemen hurrying round this corner are not going home. Follow them west.

stage.caption: A cab horse clops past on Indiana Avenue, and a gentleman on the corner checks his watch and turns west.

cast.name: A cabman waiting for a fare (unnamed)

stops.text: Indiana Avenue, a block west. Keep walking and in three more blocks there is Dearborn Street, and at 2131 and 2133 Dearborn, the Everleigh Club. Its owners are two sisters, Ada and Minna. They say they are from Kentucky; that was "another story concocted by the sisters". They were born Simms, in Virginia, in 1864 and 1866. With about $35,000 they ran a house in Omaha, then came to Chicago and bought out a madam's house on Dearborn. They took a new name from their grandmother, who signed her letters "Everly yours". The club opened on 1 February 1900, and on the first night they turned many callers away. In this business, the Everleighs understood, saying no is how you make a price.

stage.caption: Two maids hurry home along Indiana Avenue at dusk, keeping close to the houses.

stops.text: Further south along Indiana, with the Levee two blocks west. Inside the Everleigh Club are fifty rooms across two mansions: a Japanese Throne Room, a Mirror Room, a Silver Parlor, "a $15,000 gold-leafed piano for the Music Room" and "$650 gold cuspidors". A bottle of champagne costs $12, "in an era when an entire meal could be had for fifty cents", and the entrance fee alone is $50. Ada keeps the books and hires the women. Minna meets the guests. In March 1902 Prince Henry of Prussia came, and when a slipper flew off during a dance and spilled champagne, one of his party drank from it, and a whole custom began. The club keeps 15 to 25 cooks and maids, and its women are called "butterflies".

stage.caption: A family comes out of the church hall into the dusk while a cab goes by the other way.

stops.text: First Presbyterian Church, at Indiana and Twenty-first Street. It stands at the Levee's eastern edge, close enough to hear it on a summer night. The club's famed clients, the stories say, include the actor John Barrymore and the authors Ring Lardner and Theodore Dreiser, and gossips name the young Marshall Field Jr., who lives a few blocks from here, among them. "A rival madam maliciously accused the Everleigh sisters" of far worse, later, and the rumour never died. The minister's door is lit. So is the club's. Tonight, as every night, the Levee is busier.

title: The Sisters of the Levee
